title: How I used AI to create pixel arts. Cyberfarm: back to dirt!
author: mattb-it
selftext:
Hi,

My name is Matt and I've been working on this game for many months. I'm not a designer, but software developer and I've been working for last 15 years mostly as web/desktop developer. I love games and I always dreamed of creating my own one.

The problem was always the same - art/graphic design. I had many ideas, good understanding of code, but zero knowledge about pixel art. But AI changed A LOT. I use Claude Code for 2 years and I started also using Codex for last couple of months. I vibe-coded my own local-hosted Sprite Studio. Application built using Node (for UI) and Python (for sprites generation). I use Google NanoBanana and OpenAI GPT image 2. I created 90% of pixel art in this game using my own vibe-coded tool that uses AI. That's crazy. I know there are many things to improve in animations and sprites, but I'm happy with current results. Game is playable, graphics understandable and I can validate my game before diving deep into pro-graphics.

https://preview.redd.it/bnme3sd1dobh1.png?width=694&format=png&auto=webp&s=9c36624d057fbc5cc2502dba18a29a27a43c071a

https://preview.redd.it/usvlmrd1dobh1.png?width=1118&format=png&auto=webp&s=0dd2e4336ad740529116c98408072f2bd9811ac2

https://preview.redd.it/hq5fjbe1dobh1.png?width=1074&format=png&auto=webp&s=1370f97d67e8246aeb81709da8e6fe415e43176d

https://preview.redd.it/vlj4mee1dobh1.png?width=1607&format=png&auto=webp&s=bab678bc83fdb0fa4b1e27fdce245cc2408826cc

This is a cozy-but-dangerous blend of farming sim, factory builder and base defense, in a handcrafted 2.5D world where pixel-art terrain meets real-time 3D machines with aliens and a neon terminal interface.

Current state of game allows you to play at least couple of hours! Before running the game you can select difficulty level.

Link to the game -> [https://mattbit.itch.io/cyberfarm](https://mattbit.itch.io/cyberfarm)

comments.author: loontoon
comments.body:
I'll be checking this out when I'm at my desk. 

Similar background to you, I used to build websites but haven't had a single job in 18 months so I decided I'd use my skills writing technical specifications, and managing designers and developers, but instead manage AI to create the game idea I had.

replies.author: mattb-it
replies.body:
Good luck! But don't let AI write all of your code. I've found that it tends to make more bad decisions and introduce more code smells as a project grows. The first few hours of development and the initial features usually look great, but once the codebase gets larger, AI often starts implementing features in strange places. Instead of reusing existing code, it tends to recreate almost the same mechanics from scratch. And yeah, I used different skills/prompts/workflows and I always end with similar results.

I also wanted to learn Godot, so I decided not to use AI to write the code.

replies.author: loontoon
replies.body:
I've been quite lucky, the code has been very good, probably because I understand how large projects are structured and I'm given AI (Claude, Qwen and Big Pickle) small modular tasks, rather than one big job. I documented everything first so it understood the project before writing any code. 

Today I instructed Fable to review the entire codebase for the game and the level editor, and told it to look through all the GitHub and all the various documents, and then tell me what code issues it finds and any other issues. 

Fable reported back "The engineering is in decent shape — clean scripts, no leaked secrets, working save/
analytics/editor infrastructure." 

Then it made some optimisation suggestions that whilst not absolutely necessary are good coming practices. 

However, I appreciate what you mean. 

I feel that my years managing development teams puts me in a better position to direct AI than someone without that experience.

replies.author: mattb-it
replies.body: I generated some assets like rocks, trees, bushes using my sprite studio. I implemented some of them as individual scenes in Godot, but most of them are just tiles without any collisions. Then I purchased some tilesets to create "ground" and I created map "by hand" manually in Godot painting around tile layers. I only used Fable to generate paths sprites.

comments.author: captain_proton
comments.body: Cool! I'm thinking of creating my own Pixel Studio type thing too. Any tips?

replies.author: mattb-it
replies.body:
Both Nano Banana and GPT Image 2.0 can generate images only in high resolution, it is impossible to generate pixel arts. So you will need to create a lot of post-processing to pixelify it and make it readable. The biggest issue are smallest ones. The ones that have 16px as height or width. It is almost impossible to generate such pixel graphic that is readable. You can do it, but you will end up fixing it manually.

I also struggle with animations. My Sprite Studio cannot create proper walking animation. It is ok to generate mining/watering animation, but loop animations (ping-pong) are difficult. I found that most of common pixel art generators are using the same engine under the hood for animations - [https://pixelengine.ai](https://pixelengine.ai) \- it seems to be really accurate. They have an API, but it seems expensive.

So maybe not tips, but rather my observations where I struggled most: small pixel art and animations.
